newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Telecom Italia Mobile optimistic on 1996.
newsitem.headline: Telecom Italia Mobile optimistic on 1996.

text.p: Telecom Italia Mobile (TIM) forecast on Monday that its 1996 results would be in line with those of the first half, when pretax profits jumped 48 percent.
"We are confident we will follow in this direction (for the whole year)," CEO Vito Gamberale told a news briefing.

Presenting an optimistic assessment of Europe's largest mobile phone operator, he also said that the company's GSM digital services had broken even in the first half of the year and had made 100 billion lire in gross profits during the first nine months.
"It means we are the first mobile operator (in Europe) in the first year of services that was able to break even," Gamberale said, referring to the 12 months from June 1995.
Gamberale and Mauro Sentinelli, TIM deputy director general, attributed the company's success to its relatively low tariffs, international investments, strong distribution chain and "private nature".
While TIM, which was spun off from Telecom Italia in July 1995, is partially privatised, a majority stake is still held by state-controlled telecoms holding group STET.
But Gamberale said the company, which has more than 4.5 million subscribers, was far ahead of Deutsche Telekom or France Telecom in its privatisation efforts.

Gamberale said he was not worried about Italy's plans to license a third mobile phone operator to compete with TIM and Omnitel, controlled by information technology group Olivetti. He said that would help Italy's mobile market evolve earlier.

He said he was also unconcerned about plans by Telecom Italia to launch an advanced cordless phone based on the Digital European Cordless Telphony (DECT) standard. That could help lure more customers away from fixed telephone networks, he said.
"We think DECT will give all people the possibility to test mobile services," he said.

Italy's antitrust watchdog has criticised Telecom Italia's plan, warning that it could impede competition. Its president said the company could use its legal monopoly over Italy's fixed telephone network to compete head on with mobile operators.
TIM reported a pretax profit of 955 billion lire in the first half of 1996, a 48 percent rise on profits made in the last five-1/2 months of 1995 -- the period immediately following its spinoff.

Sentinelli said Italy's mobile market was expected to grow to more than 12 million subscribers by the end of the century. He said TIM was also targeting central Europe, China, India and South America.
